title: Question: stream isolation guidance for an embedded Arti client carrying both Nostr relay and Zcash light-wallet traffic on mobile
description:
Hello,

I am building Shielded Mesh, a fork of bitchat (iOS and Android) that embeds Arti in-process, as bitchat already does. I am not seeking funding, press or users. Please relabel or close this if a question is not appropriate for the tracker.

The app sends two kinds of traffic over Arti: Nostr relay websockets, and Zcash light-wallet sync (gRPC to lightwalletd servers). I want to stop an exit or a server from linking a user's messaging identity to their wallet activity through shared circuits.

Questions:

1. Is it the recommended Arti API pattern to use separate isolation groups (IsolationToken or equivalent) for each traffic class, and possibly per Nostr identity?
2. Are there known costs or pitfalls with keeping several isolated long-lived streams open on mobile (battery, circuit build limits, background suspension on iOS)?

Full design note available on request.

Thank you,
Rita, Planetary Perspective

title: guards.json corrupted to be empty after phone crash
description:
Ran into this through tor vpn, but was told to make an issue here about it since it's probably a problem here.

Phone randomly rebooted for an unknown reason, and when it came back up, tor vpn wouldn't start, and the logs point to a probably existent but empty `guards.json` (which, for reference, the guards is handled by `tor-guardmgr`, the json handled by `tor-persist`'s FsStateMgr, and the file overwrite handled by https://docs.rs/fs-mistrust/0.16.0/fs_mistrust/struct.FileAccess.html#method.write_and_replace

(my personal theory is `fs_mistrust`'s `write_and_replace` isn't quite atomic in the case of filesystem crashes. that or it's filesystem corruption on the phone end (pixel 6a, grapheneos). one strategy to prove that might be to write a test program that hammers a given store with writes, then checks that after a hard reboot nothing went wrong?)

title: tor-hsservice: duplicate reupload timers make descriptor republishing grow with uptime
description:
### Summary

The descriptor publisher keeps `reupload_timers` as a `BinaryHeap<ReuploadTimer>` and pushes a new
60-120 minute timer for a time period after every upload round, without removing the earlier timer
for that period. Each timer that fires triggers a full reupload, which pushes another timer. So every
*extra* upload round (an IPT change, a network change, a failed round - a "0/N HSDirs" round pushes a
timer too) leaves behind a timer that keeps rescheduling itself, and the reupload rate grows with how
long the service has been running. Timers only merge when one fires while an upload for its period is
already pending.

The field already carries a TODO describing this
(`crates/tor-hsservice/src/publish/reactor.rs`, from !1971):

> Currently, if, for some reason, we upload the descriptor multiple times for the same TP, we will
> end up with multiple ReuploadTimer entries for that TP, each of which will (eventually) result in
> a reupload.

I couldn't find an issue for it, and the effect turned out to be large on a phone.

### What we saw

An Android app (Night Drop) running an onion service with arti 0.43.0, overnight on mobile data,
screen off, with diagnostic logging:

- "descriptor reupload timer elapsed" went from about 1/hour after a start to **28-36/hour** after
  ~20 hours of uptime.
- HSDir uploads followed: **200-270/hour**, with arti's 1-minute publish rate limit hit 86 times in
  one night.
- The log shows the pattern directly, e.g. "reuploading descriptor in 1h 9m" followed by "descriptor
  reupload timer elapsed" 16 seconds, 47 seconds and 4.5 minutes later: older timers firing back to
  back.
- A restart clears the heap, so the effect resets and slowly comes back.

With the change below, on the same phone, same conditions and uptime: timer firings **0.3/hour**,
the app's upload traffic **-72%**, its battery use **-41%**.

### Reproduction

A test in `publish.rs` using the existing mock-runtime harness: six upload rounds (IPT changes two
minutes apart, past the rate limit), then 24 hours of mock time, counting reupload rounds. A correct
publisher reuploads every 60-120 minutes, i.e. 12-24 rounds a day (25 allowing for the timer already
pending).

- Without the fix: **fails with 66 reupload rounds in 24 h** on current `main` (83320e1), 51 on 0.43.0.
- With the fix: passes, ten runs out of ten (random seeds).

### Proposed fix

When scheduling a period's reupload, drop any earlier timer for the same period first, so the heap
holds at most one entry per period:

```rust
inner
    .reupload_timers
    .retain(|timer| timer.period != time_period);
inner.reupload_timers.push(ReuploadTimer { period: time_period, when: reupload_when });
```

`BinaryHeap::retain` is O(n), and n is at most the number of time periods. The `HashMap<TimePeriod,
Instant>` the TODO suggests would also work; this is the smaller change. I have the full patch with that regression test ready (a `git diff` against `main` at 83320e1);
the crate's tests pass with it. Happy to post it here or open a merge request, whichever you prefer.

title: tor-netdoc: Slow bootstrap due to backtrace capture every time a microdescriptor is parsed
description:
## Summary

Every time a microdescriptor is parsed, even when parsing succeeds, a backtrace capture occurs, slowing down bootstrap.

On Tor VPN 1.9.1Beta (Google Play), connecting takes approximately 10 seconds even with a cached directory.

## Cause

It was discovered using simpleperf that the execution time is being spent on (MicrodescAndHash::parse → … → Bug::new_inner → Backtrace::create).

main (83320e134) crates/tor-netdoc/src/doc/microdesc.rs:413

```rust
.ok_or(internal!("chopped utf8"))
```

The argument of `ok_or()` is evaluated eagerly, so even on success, Backtrace::force_capture() is executed.

This was introduced in 9587e70a6 (!4142, tor-netdoc 0.44.0, arti 2.5.0 and later) when `&s[a..b]` was replaced with `s.get()` to avoid a panic.

There are six other places with the same pattern.

## Proposed fix

With `ok_or_else`, because the closure is only called when `get()` returns `None`, you can avoid the expensive backtrace capture.

```rust
.ok_or_else(|| internal!("chopped utf8"))
```

## Measurement

Using Tor VPN:

1. Press Connect and wait until it connects (this fills the cache).
2. Press Stop VPN, then press Reconnect (measure this step).
3. Repeat step 2 three times.

I measured the time between the log lines `Onionmasq_runProxy` and `Loaded a good directory from cache`.

In my self-built version, only `crates/tor-netdoc/src/doc/microdesc.rs:413` was modified for comparison.

- Tor VPN (Google Play) 1.9.1Beta: 9.9 / 9.1 / 9.0 seconds
- Tor VPN built from source (onionmasq 849a8d1, tor-netdoc 0.46.0):
  - Before fix: 10.0 / 9.0 / 9.1 seconds
  - After fix: 3.3 / 2.1 / 2.1 seconds
- Device: SO-52C
- OS: Android 14

title: http-connect fails to build unless the rpc feature is also enabled (2.4.0+)
description:
**Title:** `http-connect fails to build unless the rpc feature is also enabled (2.4.0+)`

### Summary

`crates/arti` does not compile with `http-connect` enabled and `rpc` disabled.

`ProxyContext::tor_client` became `Arc<TorClient<R>>` in 3cb880f30 ("Make all
TorClient constructors wrap the TorClient in an Arc.", 2026-05-13). The
`#[cfg(feature = "rpc")]` copy of `find_conn_target` was updated to match, but
the `#[cfg(not(feature = "rpc"))]` copy directly below it still returns a plain
`TorClient<R>`.

### Affected versions

First broken release is 2.4.0; 2.3.0 and earlier build fine. Still present in
2.5.0 and on main (d3cc16119, 2026-07-29).

### Steps to reproduce

```
cargo build -p arti --no-default-features --features tokio,rustls,http-connect
```

Any feature set containing `http-connect` and not `rpc` reproduces it.

### Error

```
error[E0308]: mismatched types
   --> crates/arti/src/proxy/http_connect.rs:453:12
    |
453 |         Ok(context.tor_client.clone())
    |         -- ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected `TorClient<R>`,
    |         |                             found `Arc<TorClient<R>>`
    |         arguments to this enum variant are incorrect
```

### Suggested fix

```diff
--- a/crates/arti/src/proxy/http_connect.rs
+++ b/crates/arti/src/proxy/http_connect.rs
@@ fn find_conn_target<R: Runtime>(
     context: &ProxyContext<R>,
     rpc_target: Option<&str>,
-) -> Result<arti_client::TorClient<R>, HttpConnectError> {
+) -> Result<Arc<arti_client::TorClient<R>>, HttpConnectError> {
     if rpc_target.is_some() {
         Err(HttpConnectError::NoRpcSupport)
     } else {
-        Ok(context.tor_client.clone())
+        Ok(Arc::clone(&context.tor_client))
     }
 }
```

`Arc` is already in scope in that file, and the sole caller only uses the result
through `Deref` (`client.connect_with_prefs(..)`), so nothing else needs to
change. `find_conn_target` is private, so there is no semver impact and no
`semver.md` entry is needed.

Verified by building for `aarch64-linux-android` with
`tokio,rustls,http-connect,dns-proxy,static-sqlite,bridge-client,pt-client`.

### The more useful part: nothing builds this combination

The one-line fix matters less than the gap it points at. `http-connect` is
experimental and is presumably always built alongside `rpc`, so the
`not(rpc)` branch appears never to be compiled anywhere in CI — which is how
this reached a second release unnoticed. A CI job building `http-connect`
without `rpc` would catch the next occurrence. This may be adjacent to #2545
("Crates expose more features than intended").

### Licensing

This suggested change may be used under the MIT or Apache-2.0 licence, per
CONTRIBUTING.md.

### Context

Found while building arti for an Android SOCKS5/HTTP-CONNECT proxy app, which
selects features explicitly and has no use for `rpc`.

title: try_lock is not supported on Android
description:
I am cross compiling Arti (https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti.git) on linux to make a static arm64 executable for android API 24. There are two dependencies that must also be built static which are openssl and sqlite3 libraries. Everything builds, but when I run Arti on Termux, I get the following error:

./arti: error: tor: could not read/write persistent state: Error setting up the persistent state manager: IO error while constructing storage manager on state.lock in ${HOME}/arti/data: try_lock() not supported

title: Reinstate the kqueue backend in FileWatcher
description:
In #1644, we discovered the `FileWatcher` implementation (used for watching config source files and directories for changes) does not work properly on FreeBSD and macOS because of a bug in `notify`'s kqueue-based backend: https://github.com/notify-rs/notify/issues/644

As a temporary workaround, we switched to using [`PollWatcher`](https://docs.rs/notify/latest/notify/poll/struct.PollWatcher.html) on all platforms other than windows, linux, and android (we're not sure if the `FileWatcher` behaves correctly on windows, but we know that it works well with the `inotify` backend. If the default windows backend turns out to be broken as well, we can replace it with a polling watcher too).

The polling watcher is less efficient than the native alternative (it periodically re-reads the watched files/directories to see if they changed), so it's not an ideal long-term solution. We should try to reinstate the `kqueue` backend for macOS and *BSD, or implement our own `kqueue` watcher.

To do so, we could 
  * patch `notify`'s kqueue watcher implementation to better approximate inotify behavior when watching non-recursively. When adding a directory to the non-recursive watch list, it'll need to take note of all the files in that directory. When receiving a kqueue "write" event for that directory, it will need to "diff" the previous state of the directory with the current one, and emit an event for each file/directory that has changed. This is of course racy, because you could modify the contents of the directory after adding the directory to the watch list, but *before* starting the watcher.
  * implement a simpler version of the `FileWatcher` that's less strict about event handling: we can tolerate some spurious config reloads, so we could perhaps our `kqueue` replacement could be less smart (it won't need to accurately fill out the `notify::Event` with the paths that triggered the event, because we don't really care about those. We just need to know whether to re-read the config, so a simple "something changed" event would suffice). This will involve simplifying the `FileWatcher` logic too (it currently suppresses any events that aren't related to the exact files/directories the user set a watch for).

title: Failure to resolve XDG dirs produces unhelpful error messages
description:
### To reproduce

Mangle your entry in /etc/passwd so getpwuid will fail.
Run `env - target/debug/arti proxy`

### Expected output

An error message explaining that your home directory could not be determined because your uid doesn't appear to be listed in the password database.  (Similarly, other kinds of trouble should be properly reported too.)

### Actual output

> `target/debug/arti: error: identify default config file locations: Couldn't determine XDG Project Directories, needed to resolve a path; probably, unable to determine HOME directory`

(assuming !1480 is merged)

### Analysis

The error message is from `tor_config::path::Error::NoProjectDirs`, which is a unit variant.  It is a unit variant because we are using `directories` to find the XDG directories (eg, the config directory) and `directories` doesn't return errors but just says `None`.

I have filed [upstream ticket #85](https://github.com/dirs-dev/directories-rs/issues/85) for the API problem in `directories`.

This error is generated on Android if the default configuration paths are ever used, because `directories` returns `None` on Android.  That's [upstream ticket #83](https://github.com/dirs-dev/directories-rs/issues/83).  (For this reason I have added the Sponsor 101 label which seemed the best one to represent that this affects Android.)

Our options would seem to be:
 1. Use something else instead of `directories`.  I investigated and at the time of writing the only libraries that do better at this are `microxdg` and `xdg`, and even those give rather vague error messages.
 2. Use a default value of our own if `directories` says `None`.  This seems hazardous.
 3. Work on this upstream in `directories` or one of the competitor crates (look for `directories-next` and `dirs`, too).

title: TROVE-2023-001: [from security@torproject.org] DoS via infinite loop in Socks protocol implementation
description:
Received the following email on security@torproject.org:

# Issue description

The Socks protocol implementation in Arti will read from the socket to a
1024-bytes buffer in a loop. After reading from the socket, the packet is
parsed via `handshake.handshake`, which will return the following values:

* `Ok(Ok(action))`: Valid data received
* `Ok(Err(e))`: Data is invalid, close connection
* `Err(_)`: Data is truncated/not yet fully read from socket

In the case of truncated data, the loop will read from the socket again, up to
the 1024-bytes length of the buffer. After that, `handshake.handshake` is
called again, possibly repeatedly until enough data has been received:

https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti/-/blob/main/crates/arti/src/socks.rs#L119-157

If `handshake.handshake` returns `Err(_)` even if the buffer is already full,
the implementation will try to read zero bytes (`in_buf[1024..]` is an empty
buffer), which will instantly finish. After this reading attempt, the code
will try parsing the same data again, effectively resulting in an infinite
loop. This can be triggered via the (null-terminated) username or hostname
string in Socks4:

https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti/-/blob/main/crates/tor-socksproto/src/handshake/proxy.rs#L112

https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti/-/blob/main/crates/tor-socksproto/src/handshake/proxy.rs#L121

# PoC

The following PoC will connect to 127.0.0.1:9150 and send a payload to exploit
this issue:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import socket


def main():
    s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 9150))
    f = s.makefile('rwb')
    buf = b"".join([
        b"\x04",  # Socks version 4
        b"\x01",  # SocksCmd::CONNECT
        b"\x1337",  # Port, doesn't matter
        b"\x7f\x00\x00\x01",  # IP Addr, doesn't matter
        b"A" * 1024  # Username
    ])
    buf = buf[0:1024]  # Truncate it to 1024 bytes
    f.write(buf)
    f.flush()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

In order to cause full DoS against the arti binary, this exploit will need to
be run multiple times. Each run of the exploit will result in one thread in an
infinite loop and effectively block one thread of the tokio runtime. The
number of available threads defaults to the number of available CPUs and once
all these threads are stuck in an infinite loop, the arti binary will be
totally unresponsive.

# Risk

Attackers able to reach the Socks port of Arti can cause DoS. Since the Socks
port is by default only reachable on localhost, the risk is relatively low.
However, there are a couple of situations where this could still be exploited:
* Untrusted software running on the local machine, possibly in a sandboxed
environment (for example Android Apps or certain software plugins) can still
have unlimited network communication to localhost.
* Arti used as a Tor gateway to provide Tor for other machines, i.e. on a
Raspberry Pi.

# Mitigation suggestion

Abort socks handling loop if `handshake.handshake` returns `Err(_)` (which
means that more input data is expected) even though the input buffer has
already been fully received (up to the 1024 byte limit).

CC: @nickm @Diziet @gabi-250

title: Bootstrap event sender doesn't always report readiness correctly
description:
It's unclear whether this is working as intended or not, but it appears that loading a bootstrapped directory successfully from cache won't go and update the bootstrap status reported through `BootstrapEvents` as hitting 100%. The most I managed to get it to was 

```
2023-03-28T15:26:53.339788Z DEBUG arti_client::status: 45%: connecting successfully; directory is fetching authority certificates (8/8)
```

Since it never sets `ready_for_traffic` either, consumers depending on the bootstrap event sender might mistakenly think that bootstrap is still ongoing.

You can work around this in client code by calling `TorClient::bootstrap` manually and reporting completion when that function returns, but it'd be nice to have the event sender fixed;

- it seems weird that `TorClient::bootstrap` can return without `ready_for_traffic` also being set;
- and it seems weird that you will only see the 100% bootstrap event state when downloading a fresh directory.

(arti 1.1.2 installed via Cargo on Linux, but the problem also happens embedded on Android)

title: Failure to bootstrap due to cache directory problems results in a bad end-user experience
description:
### Summary

While working on onionmasq, I encountered a problem with the Arti client failing to bootstrap. After some investigation, this appeared to be related to an issue with the cache. Deleting the cache entirely and restarting fixed things up, but the end-user experience here was lacking, especially in the context of integrating Arti as a library.

### Steps to reproduce:

1. Something weird happens to the cache directory
2. The Arti client no longer works

### What is the current bug behavior?

I got the following error message on calling `bootstrap()` which was resoundingly unhelpful:

```
onion_tunnel: Failed to bootstrap: tor: cache access problem: Unable to bootstrap a working directory
```

I then realised (given insider knowledge) that I had to format out the causes, and got this:

```
onion_tunnel: Caused by: Unable to bootstrap a working directory
onion_tunnel: Caused by: Bad permissions in cache directory
onion_tunnel: Caused by: File or directory /data/user/0/org.torproject.artitoyvpn/cache/arti-cache/dir_blobs/con_microdesc_sha3-256-339e2da5279de87281cfd59f0b3d0f324a15045a8540e9a71a396d68c3e74d54 not found
```

There are a number of issues here (see below).

### What is the expected behavior?

- Bootstrapping should be able to gracefully deal with cache directory problems, without user intervention
  - When embedding Arti, this just looks like the entire thing is irreparably broken, when in fact it's a transient issue that could be easily resolved by clearing the cache
  - Users can't always do this themselves if Arti is embedded, nor would they necessarily receive indication that they need to.
  - The embedding library can't do it without relying on API-unstable error munging tactics, since no machine-readable API is exposed to ascertain that the cache dir is at fault
- The error should be correctly categorized; this doesn't look like a permissions issue
  - The top-level error could possibly be renamed, too: I initially read 'working directory' as 'some place to put scratch files' (i.e. the Git 'working directory'), which was confusing
  - (perhaps "Unable to download a Tor network directory" or similar)
- (more opinionated, but) We should strongly consider rethinking the `Error::source` idea
  - A 'normal' embedder (who didn't work on the Arti team for a year) would have no idea how to get more information out of the error, and would assume the nondescript `Unable to bootstrap a working directory` line was it
  - There's no standard way to print an error's causes ([`std::error::Report`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/error/struct.Report.html) is still unstable)
  - Even if there was, the user might be transforming the error into an `io::Error` or something, or passing it across an FFI boundary; having to thread the error-cause thing throughout the end-user codebase is just a pointless form of make-work
  - This might make sense once the rest of the ecosystem has caught up, but right now it's a really obscure user experience

### Environment

- Version: arti-client 0.8.1 from crates.io, embedded inside onionmasq
- Operating system: Android 13

title: Allow UNmanaged instance of pluggable transport
description:
### Summary

Currently on Android apps like Orbot or OnionShare, we use UNmanaged instances of pluggable transports which we run ourselves using [IPtProxy](https://gitlab.com/guardianproject/IPtProxy). IPtProxy runs the instance of Obfs4Proxy, Snowflake, etc. in-process as true libraries, and not as executables pretending to be libraries.

This means that we configure C-Tor to use Snowflake like this:

ClientTransportPlugin snowflake socks5 127.0.0.1:9999
Bridge snowflake 192.0.2.3:1 2B280B23E1107BB62ABFC40DDCC8824814F80A72

instead of giving it a path to the executable.

For these existing apps, and the Tor VPN Android app, this will be required moving forward, as Android OS is increasingly hostile to applications bundling/hiding executables inside of them.


### What is the expected behavior?

Regarding documentation here: https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti/-/blob/main/doc/bridges.md we would hope to allow support for the following kind of configuration, either via the toml, or via the future FFI.

```
[[bridges.transports]]
protocols = ["snowflake"]
uri = "socks5://127.0.0.1:9999"
#path = "/PATH/TO/snowflake-client"
#arguments = ["-log-to-state-dir", "-log", "snowflake.log"]
arguments = []
run_on_startup = false
```
```
[bridges]

enabled = true
bridges = [
  "Bridge snowflake 192.0.2.3:1 2B280B23E1107BB62ABFC40DDCC8824814F80A72"
]
```

milestone.title: Arti:  Feature parity with the C implementation
milestone.description:
Deliverable 1: Parity with C tor client: all relevant non-deprecated C Tor client features are present.

Deliverable 2: Full embedding support: Arti exposes a set of APIs sufficient developing applications that use it in Rust and non-rust languages.

Milestone 2.0.0 for ZC

From the [grant proposal](//zcashgrants.org/gallery/25215916-53ea-4041-a3b2-6d00c487917d/29067252/):

>In time, we want Arti to become the primary Tor implementation, so that we can focus our efforts on a high-productivity, high-security program environment without all of the drawbacks of our old C implementation. But before we can do that, we need Arti to work well enough as a replacement for existing Tor users that they can migrate to it comfortably.
>
>In the second half of our second year, we will be “filling in the gaps” to make Arti 2.0.0 a better alternative to the C client implementation for nearly all users. This will include work on circuit padding, a stable C FFI, support for more proxy protocols, and whatever missing features users and developers judge to be most important.
>
>Once that’s done, we’ll be able to deprecate client usage of the C Tor implementation (though we’ll have to keep supporting it in maintenance mode for a couple of years, to give users and developers time to migrate).
> Throughout the project, we will update Arti's documentation on https://arti.torproject.org. Our goal is to make Arti easy to use for any project that would like to integrate Tor into their solution.
>
> `[...]`
>
> The greater part of this work will take the form of several new higher-level APIs, including:
>
>  * A “blocking API” layer for use by applications that can’t or won’t interface with Rust’s async futures ecosystem.
>  * A “FFI layer” to expose Arti’s functionality in a form suitable for consumption by non-Rust applications.
>  * A “compatibility layer” to support drop-in replacement use of Arti for a limited set of legacy C Tor use-cases.
